title: Gates Foundation Pledges Up to $1 Billion for Family Planning Through 2030
excerpt: Announced at the Copenhagen Summit, the commitment puts $694 million into family planning and sits on top of a separate $2.5 billion women's health research pledge from August 2025.
body:
• The Gates Foundation said Monday it plans to commit up to US$1 billion through 2030 to family planning and women's health, announced at the Copenhagen Summit on Gender Equality and Women's and Girls' Rights.
  • The planned portfolio: US$694 million for family planning, US$158 million for women's health innovations, US$50 million for maternal and child health, plus smaller allocations for health surveys and adolescent outcomes.
  • The pledge is additional to the foundation's US$2.5 billion commitment to women's health research and development announced in August 2025.
  • The foundation says more than 257 million women and girls who want to avoid pregnancy are not using a modern contraceptive method — the gap the funding is aimed at.

The Gates Foundation on Monday reaffirmed its commitment to voluntary family planning, outlining plans to commit up to US$1 billion through 2030 to expand access to contraception and support women's health. The announcement came as governments, civil society and philanthropic partners gathered in Copenhagen for the Summit on Gender Equality and Women's and Girls' Rights, where Nordic governments launched a new international partnership to sustain funding for sexual and reproductive health and rights.

"Family planning is one of the most powerful tools we have to improve outcomes for women."

— Anita Zaidi, President of Gender Equality, Gates Foundation

Where the money is pointed

The foundation's planned portfolio, set out in its Copenhagen announcement, allocates US$694 million to family planning — supporting voluntary access to contraception, quality services, country partnerships, data generation and community engagement — and US$158 million to women's health innovations. A further US$50 million goes to maternal and child health through the Global Financing Facility's Sustainable Commodities Access Program, which works on reliable access to essential health supplies, alongside US$17 million for demographic and health surveys and US$18 million for adolescent outcomes. The commitments are in addition to the US$2.5 billion the foundation pledged to women's health research and development in August 2025.

The case the foundation makes

The foundation frames family planning as central to its goal of halving maternal and child deaths by 2045. It cites more than 257 million women and girls who want to avoid pregnancy but are not using a modern contraceptive method, and says meeting that demand requires sustained investment at a time when funding is under pressure. In its release, the foundation states that rising contraceptive use prevented an estimated one in four maternal deaths in 2023, and that contraceptive use and quality pregnancy care together avert an estimated 544,000 newborn deaths annually across low- and middle-income countries. Its family planning work focuses on countries where need is greatest, supporting new contraceptive development, improved services and stronger delivery systems with governments and local organisations.

The Nordic partnership

The pledge coincides with a partnership launched at the Copenhagen Summit by Nordic governments in collaboration with philanthropic organisations. The partnership aims to sustain investment in sexual and reproductive health and rights, mobilise additional financing and support country-led priorities, including local manufacturing and supply chains for essential health products. The foundation said it will focus its engagement on family planning, maternal and child health, and access to essential health products for women in lower-income countries.

"We know that progress in maternal and child survival depends on women having access to the contraception and quality pregnancy and birthing care they want and need," Zaidi said. "This commitment is designed to help expand that access, so more women can make informed choices about their health and futures."
